title: Slab-built hanging crescent planter
subtitle: A wall-mounted crescent-shaped planter for a small succulent, with a drainage hole and cord slot
excerpt: A crescent planter is a slab-built trough curved into a crescent arc and fitted with a back wall for mounting. This version uses air-dry clay with no kiln. The finished planter is 18 cm wide and holds a 5-6 cm pot or a direct planting of a small succulent in potting grit.
sourceNotes: Technique derived from first principles. V&A open-access collection for decorative ceramic form reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to an even thickness, used as the building unit in slab construction
The stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but remains damp enough to join, trim, and carve
The joining method: roughen both surfaces with a needle tool, apply clay slip, then press together firmly
Fully air-dried and unfired; pale, lightweight, and fragile, ready for sealing
Any unfired clay piece, from freshly made through to bone-dry; the term covers the full air-drying journey before sealing

content.text: A crescent wall planter is a slab-built trough bent into a crescent arc and mounted on a flat back panel for hanging. This version is air-dry clay: no kiln, no wheel. The finished planter is 18 cm at the widest point across the arc and holds one small succulent or a 5 cm pot inside the trough.

materials.name: Clay slip (same clay body, thinned with water to double-cream consistency)
Macrame or jute cord for hanging
Waterproof exterior varnish or resin spray (for light outdoor protection)

content.text: Preparation

This is an intermediate project because the crescent trough must be bent to shape at the right moment: too soft and it slumps, too stiff and it cracks. Work in a cool room with low airflow. Prepare your clay slip before starting. Cut two guide rods or use thick pencils as rolling guides to keep the
slab

an even 7 mm throughout. Roll on a canvas sheet. Have a curved form ready to support the bent trough while it sets: a rolling pin, a thick book wrapped in cling film, or a section of PVC pipe 18-20 cm in diameter all work.
Making the trough base
Roll a slab 7 mm thick. Cut a rectangle 22 cm x 8 cm. This is the floor and front face of the trough.

A crescent wall planter is a slab-built trough bent into a curved arc. A flat back panel holds it against the wall for hanging. This version uses air-dry clay. No kiln or wheel is needed. The finished planter is 18 cm across at its widest. It holds one small succulent or a 5 cm pot in the trough.

Drape the stiffened slab over your curved support so the long axis bends into a gentle crescent arc. The outer edge of the arc should be the 22 cm length. Press the slab gently around the form so the curve is smooth. Leave to stiffen on the support for two hours.
Pierce a drainage hole 8 mm in diameter at the deepest point of the bent trough using the needle tool. This prevents standing water at the root zone.
Adding the walls and back panel

Roll a second slab 7 mm thick. Cut two end walls: follow the profile of the trough arc at each end, making each wall 8 cm tall and wide enough to close the trough section. Cut these while the trough is still on the curved support so the profiles match the actual curve.
Use needle tool and slip to
score and slip
the end walls to the trough at each end. Press firmly and blend the interior seam with a wooden rib. Support the joins from the outside with a thin clay coil while they firm.

Roll a third slab 7 mm thick. Cut a back panel to follow the outer arc of the trough: 22 cm along the curved edge, 5 cm wide at the centre. This panel mounts flat against the wall and forms the hanging point.
Score and slip the back edges of the trough and the corresponding face of the back panel. Press together and blend all joins inside and outside with a wooden rib.

Cut a cord slot through the back panel at the top centre: a rectangle 12 mm wide x 6 mm tall. Thread the hanging cord through this slot after drying and sealing. Smooth the edges of the slot with a damp finger.
Surface decoration (optional)
At the leather-hard stage, press a pottery stamp or a piece of lace into the exterior of the trough front for texture. Work from the centre outward to avoid distorting the arc.
Carve a scored line border 5 mm from the top rim of the trough with the needle tool. Two parallel lines at 3 mm spacing look clean and tidy.
Drying
Remove the trough from the curved support once the walls have reached
leather-hard
and hold their shape unaided. Place on a flat board and allow to air-dry fully. Any
greenware
piece dries better slowly: cover loosely with a thin cloth for the first 24 hours, then leave uncovered until fully
bone-dry
. Full drying takes three to four days. The piece is bone-dry when it is pale throughout, lightweight, and no longer cool to the touch.
Finishing

Apply two coats of 50/50 PVA and water to all surfaces including the interior. Allow each coat to dry between applications. For planters that will be used outdoors or in a humid greenhouse, apply an additional coat of exterior-grade spray varnish over the dried PVA. This adds moisture resistance but does not make the planter fully waterproof. Thread the cord through the slot at the back panel after sealing, then tie a knot on the interior face to hold it. Hang the planter from a hook or nail through the back panel slot.
Care

Air-dry clay is not fully waterproof even when sealed. Place a small amount of grit or fine gravel in the base of the trough before planting to aid drainage through the drainage hole. Water the succulent sparingly. Wipe the exterior with a dry cloth only. Do not leave the planter exposed to heavy rain: the clay will eventually soften through prolonged soaking even with PVA sealing.
Variations
Make the trough 30 cm across for a larger crescent that holds three succulents in a row. Increase clay weight to 800 g and allow longer drying time at each stage to avoid cracking the longer arc.

Omit the cord slot and instead score and slip two clay loop handles to the back panel at the leather-hard stage. Thread cord through both loops to create a cradle hanging at two points rather than one central slot.

Press botanical impressions into the trough front before bending: lay a fern frond or a sprig of rosemary face-down on the slab, roll lightly over with the rolling pin, then peel away to leave the impression. Do this before draping, while the slab is still flat.

items.problem: Trough cracked along the outer arc during bending
items.cause: The slab was too stiff when bent; clay at leather-hard cannot flex without cracking
items.fix: Slab bending needs to happen before leather-hard, when the clay is firm but still flexible. If cracked, dampen the crack, press closed, and support the join with a clay coil until dry

items.problem: End wall join opened up on drying
items.cause: Insufficient scoring or slip at the join, or the clay dried unevenly pulling the join apart
items.fix: At leather-hard, dampen, re-score, apply fresh slip, and press firmly closed. Wrap the whole piece loosely in plastic to slow drying and allow the join to heal

items.problem: The planter bows forward away from the wall
items.cause: The back panel was too thin or not flat enough to hold the trough weight
items.fix: Add a second layer of slab to the back panel at leather-hard to thicken it. Allow to dry fully flat, weighted with a book, before hanging

items.problem: Drainage hole blocked by clay during building
items.cause: Slip or clay dust sealed the hole during scoring or smoothing
items.fix: Re-open the hole at leather-hard with the needle tool. Check the hole is clear by holding the piece up to light before drying

items.cause: The trough was removed from the curved support before the clay was firm enough to hold the arc unaided
items.fix: Return the trough to the support and allow another two hours. If already flattened and leather-hard, you cannot re-bend; dry and seal as a shallower form
